prompt: You estimated 15 days for a feature. It's day 9 and you're about a quarter done — the legacy schema had undocumented states and the reporting library doesn't handle timezones at all. Your PM has told a customer it ships in three weeks. She asks how it's going in standup. What do you say?
answer_markdown: Say it now, that day, not at the next milestone. The arithmetic is already conclusive: a quarter done in 60% of the time is a velocity ratio around 0.42, projecting to roughly 2.7x the original estimate — you will not catch that up, and 'still on track' spends every option your PM has left. Told at day nine she can warn the customer early, cut scope, or get help; told at day nineteen she can do none of those. Bring three parts. What changed and why the original number was wrong, specifically — 'the schema has three states we had no record of and the library does not do timezones', not 'it was harder than expected'. The new range with its remaining uncertainty. And priced options: full scope at about six weeks, or ship without timezone-correct rollups in three weeks and follow up, or add a second engineer which helps only on the export half because the schema work does not parallelise. That last honesty matters — offering 'add a person' for work that cannot be split is how you get a person added and still slip. Then name what you will do differently: spike the unknown integration first next time.

prompt: Why do experienced engineers still miss estimates by large factors, and what does that mean for how you should estimate?
answer_markdown: Because early estimates are made at the point of maximum ignorance. Steve McConnell's cone of uncertainty puts initial-concept estimates off by up to 4x in either direction — a 16x total spread — and that is a property of estimating work you have not done rather than a personal failing. The crucial detail is that the cone narrows only as you make decisions that eliminate variability, not as time passes: sitting inside a project for three weeks does not improve the estimate, answering questions does. Two practical consequences follow. First, identify the two or three unknowns whose answers move the number most, and go resolve them before committing — a one-day spike on the vendor API is worth more than a week of careful decomposition around an unknown. Second, give ranges with the driver named rather than point estimates: 'two to five weeks, and the spread depends entirely on whether the vendor supports bulk export, which I can find out tomorrow' tells your PM both the number and how to shrink it.

prompt: How do you handle scope creep without becoming the engineer who says no to everything?
answer_markdown: Recognise it as a bookkeeping failure rather than a discipline problem. Nobody ever agreed to a 40% larger project — it accumulated across twelve conversations, each request individually small and easy to say yes to in ten seconds. The fix is not refusing, it is refusing to absorb silently: price each addition at the moment it arrives. 'Yes, that is about three days. It fits if we drop the CSV export, or it moves the date to the 14th — which do you prefer?' You have said yes, and you have made the cost visible and the trade explicit. In practice a large share of such requests are quietly withdrawn once they carry a price, which tells you they were never worth their cost and the requester simply had no way to know. Then make it structural by keeping a visible list of accepted changes with their day costs, so the twelfth request arrives in a room where the previous eleven are on screen. Without that list, the project is just mysteriously late and you have no way to show why.

prompt: Your director says your six-week estimate has to be four weeks because that's the customer commitment. There's no new information — just pressure. What do you say?
answer_markdown: Hold the estimate and move a different variable, out loud. An estimate that changes because of pressure rather than evidence is not an estimate, and agreeing teaches everyone that your numbers are negotiable — which means next time the negotiation starts lower. It also makes you solely responsible for closing a gap you did not create. Every project has four variables — scope, time, people, quality — and when one moves, at least one other must. So do not refuse; offer the trade: 'Six weeks is what this scope costs. To hit four we can cut the audit log and bulk import, which gets it to about four and a half; or add an engineer on the export half, which is genuinely parallelisable; or ship at four with the migration behind a flag for internal users and go external at six.' Deciding what to trade is their job, not yours. The variable to watch is quality, because it is the one that moves silently by default — if nobody explicitly chooses, the overrun comes out of testing and design and nobody ever agreed to that.

prompt: Your own estimate was accurate but a dependency from another team slipped, and now you'll miss the date. Whose problem is that?
answer_markdown: Still yours to renegotiate, and this question is testing ownership. 'Blocked on another team' is a status, not an excuse, and the immediate follow-up is what you did about it: did you flag the dependency as a risk at the start, did you check in on their progress rather than assuming, did you look for a way to unblock or work around it, and did you re-forecast your own date as soon as theirs moved? The commitment your stakeholders are planning against is yours, so the communication obligation does not transfer even though the delay was not caused by you. What sounds weak in an interview is describing the dependency as something that happened to you; what sounds senior is describing when you first knew it was at risk and what you did in between. If the answer is that you found out the week it was due, the real finding is that you were not tracking a dependency you knew your delivery sat on.

prompt: Is it better to pad your estimates or give an honest number?
answer_markdown: Hidden padding is the worst of the options, because it gets found and removed. Once a manager learns your numbers contain buffer, they discount every future estimate — including the ones that had none — and you end up padding to compensate for the discount, which is a spiral. The alternative is not naive optimism, it is stating a range with an explicit driver: 'four to seven days, depending on whether the migration needs a backfill, which I will know by tomorrow.' That communicates genuine uncertainty honestly and survives scrutiny, because there is nothing hidden to find. It also puts the uncertainty in the right place — a range invites the useful question 'what would it take to narrow that?' whereas a padded point estimate invites 'can you do it faster?' Buffer at the project level, held openly by whoever owns the schedule, is legitimate and normal; buffer smuggled inside individual task estimates is a credibility problem waiting to happen.
